proposals.name: Form mirrors content
proposals.instruction: Score high if the story's structural or formal choice (fragmented syntax, found-document framing, list format, verse, unusual punctuation, tense/person choice) is itself an expressive device that enacts or reinforces the story's central idea, rather than being a neutral default container for the plot. Score low if the prose form is generic past-tense narration with no relationship between how it's told and what it's about.
proposals.rationale: R17's stuttering, miscounted sentences ('1, 2, 3. 1, 2, 3... 24. Sorry. 24.') formally enact the time-loop's disorientation; R09's in-universe 'Containment Protocol' extract framing suits its documentary-history concept; R29's clipped, ellipsis-heavy lines mirror the narrator's chemically numbed affect. None of these would score on a checklist that only asks 'is the prose competent.'

proposals.name: Final line lands
proposals.instruction: Score high if the story's last sentence or image delivers a genuine turn, thematic closure, or emotional payoff that recontextualizes what came before. Score low if the piece simply stops, trails into a generic action, or ends on a beat unconnected to any throughline established earlier.
proposals.rationale: R14 ('Sixteen generations. Gods damn it, I would have to fly.') and R31 ('To serve is the highest honour.') both close a full emotional arc opened in their first lines. By contrast R39 ends on an inert shopkeeper's warning ('This stuff'll make you hallucinate') that never resolves or reframes the blinking-statue setup at all.

proposals.name: Sustained distinctive voice
proposals.instruction: Score high if the narration maintains one controlled, recognizable persona/register throughout (diction, rhythm, and attitude stay coherent even as events change). Score low if the register is generic, or if it drifts inconsistently without apparent purpose.
proposals.rationale: R18 sustains an ornate, ironic essayistic voice ('the garnish on the grand dish of economic maneuvering') for its entire length; R32, despite being paratext rather than fiction, still carries a warm, consistent first-person community voice ('we do miss challenges, much to our regret'). Contrast R30, which has no voice at all -- it is a templated notice ('This is an automated message').

proposals.name: Idea extends past the literal prompt
proposals.instruction: Score high if the story develops a twist, irony, or insight that reframes the prompt's premise into something the prompt didn't hand the writer -- an idea that couldn't be guessed just from reading the prompt. Score low if the story answers the prompt literally and stops, with no further conceptual move.
proposals.rationale: R09 turns 'humans are terrifyingly bold' into a specific mechanism (loud confidence reads as having 'jumped the technological barrier,' so predators flee), and R40 has the student's follow-up push the Schrodinger's-cat thought experiment somewhere new (the geiger counter as an internal observer). R11, by contrast, just juxtaposes a death text with vapid chatter and never develops that juxtaposition into anything further.

proposals.name: Stakes are dramatized, not just asserted
proposals.instruction: Score high if danger, loss, or urgency is rendered through scene-level sensory/psychological detail the reader feels in the moment. Score low if a character simply states the stakes in dialogue or narration ('this is very dangerous') without the scene making the reader feel it.
proposals.rationale: R06's fragmented first-person confusion ('Who are all these assholes standing around me?! ... Wait, what's happened to my home?') makes disorientation viscerally felt rather than described. R33 instead has a character explain the danger in an expository speech ('This entire facility has only one set of power matrices. If they go, so does the colony... We're talking about a thermonuclear bomb') -- told, not dramatized.

proposals.name: Exposition earns its place through wit or insight
proposals.instruction: Score high if passages of narration/summary (as opposed to scene-with-dialogue) contain real stylistic invention, aphorism, or conceptual density that rewards reading them closely. Score low if expository passages are purely functional information-delivery with no distinctive phrasing.
proposals.rationale: R18 is almost entirely exposition yet is dense with quotable wit ('akin to arriving at a masquerade already unmasked'). R33's opening exposition about the atmospheric processor's four functions is competent but purely functional, with no comparable payoff sentence-by-sentence.

proposals.name: Constitutes an actual story
proposals.instruction: Score high if the text contains a recognizable narrative unit: at least one character, a situation, and some forward motion or change, sustained for more than a single beat. Score low if the text is not fiction at all (an announcement, a removal notice) or is a single unelaborated line with no scene, character, or development.
proposals.rationale: R30 is a moderator's automated post-removal notice with zero narrative content, and R37 is a two-sentence gag with no scene ever staged. Contrast R01, which has setup, confrontation, and resolution across a full scene.

proposals.name: Purposeful use of shocking or transgressive material
proposals.instruction: Score high if violent, sexual, or grotesque content is deployed in service of a legible narrative or thematic point, with the story doing something with the shock. Score low if graphic content appears to exist for its own sake, disconnected from any throughline, or is undercut by a flippant tag that signals the writer wasn't taking their own material seriously.
proposals.rationale: R04 escalates body-horror imagery into a genuine (if unsettling) meditation on human/alien difference, while R13 repeats a gory dismemberment beat purely as a punchline, closing with a chipper 'Well...that was fun :)' that treats its own violence as disposable. Judges should be asked to weigh whether the darkness is doing narrative work.

proposals.name: Fresh handling of a familiar trope
proposals.instruction: Score high if the story takes a well-worn genre trope (monster under the bed, thought-experiment classroom scene, curse reversal, etc.) and complicates, subverts, or extends it in a way a reader wouldn't already expect. Score low if the trope is executed exactly as genre convention predicts, with no additional turn.
proposals.rationale: R01's big-sister-defeats-the-closet-monster is a competently executed but wholly conventional rendition of its trope with no surprise in how it resolves. R40 instead takes the very familiar Schrodinger's-cat classroom bit and has the student's question genuinely complicate the thought experiment (the geiger counter as internal observer), giving the trope a new wrinkle.

proposals.name: Psychological specificity of the POV character
proposals.instruction: Score high if the protagonist's interior life is rendered through specific, idiosyncratic thoughts or details unique to that character, not generic emotion labels. Score low if the character's feelings are only named/asserted from outside ('he was furious') rather than textured from within.
proposals.rationale: R06's dementia patient thinks in very specific fragments ('Beatrice never liked green. Why are the curtains green?'), and R23's Lijah has a petty, specific grudge ('If Davidson'd been sent here, he'd be drowning in mystical energy... What do I get? A pissin' hole with bad breath'). Contrast R24's Joffrey, whose anger is only reported externally ('His head was shaking with rage').

proposals.name: Escalation across the piece
proposals.instruction: Score high if tension, stakes, or the character's situation meaningfully changes or intensifies from the story's opening to its close. Score low if the piece stays at one note throughout, essentially repeating its opening gambit without development.
proposals.rationale: R14 escalates through distinct stages (waiting, hatching, the physical struggle to bridle the dragon) and R07 develops Mason's insecurity across the scene. R05, by contrast, repeats nearly the same beat twice almost verbatim (licking the wall, then licking the floor) with no development between them, and R08's banter stays flat from start to finish.

proposals.name: Sentence-level freshness vs. cliche phrasing
proposals.instruction: Score high if sentences contain apt, unexpected imagery or phrasing that couldn't be swapped into any other story. Score low if the prose leans on stock phrases and off-the-shelf genre diction ('dead meat,' 'evil clutches,' 'how dare you').
proposals.rationale: R18 repeatedly produces original figurative language ('eating the decorative swan at a banquet before it has had time to preen itself'), while R28 ('I'd just break theirs, physically') and R24 ('How dare you compare me... the audacity!') rely on generic, interchangeable genre phrasing.

proposals.name: Stands alone without outside context
proposals.instruction: Score high if everything needed to understand the characters, relationships, and stakes is present on the page. Score low if the story depends on knowledge from a linked prior installment or other external material the reader isn't given, leaving relationships or references unexplained.
proposals.rationale: R21 explicitly frames itself as 'a continuation of a series of earlier prompt responses' with an external link, and the reader is given no explanation for who Marley is or why she can rescue Charley. R14 and R31, though both imply larger worlds, give the reader everything needed within the text itself.

proposals.name: Restraint from authorial glossing
proposals.instruction: Score high if the story's meaning or joke is conveyed entirely through the narrative itself, trusting the reader to get it. Score low if the writer appends an explanatory comment after the story ends that spells out the theme or punchline for the reader.
proposals.rationale: R35 closes its narrative beat ('Pub.' 'Pub.') but then adds an out-of-story editorial line explaining the joke ('Nothing like a little wholesome necromancy'), undercutting the reader's own inference. R09 instead lets its irony (a council of species electing to hide from noisy, confident humans) stand entirely on its own with no appended gloss.

proposals.name: Specificity of physical action choreography
proposals.instruction: Score high if physical action is tracked with clear, sequential, embodied detail (specific body parts, positions, cause-and-effect motion) that lets a reader stage the action mentally. Score low if action is conveyed in generic, summary-style beats (a list of things happening) without embodied specificity.
proposals.rationale: R14 choreographs the dragon-taming with exact physical sequence ('I slowly fed my right arm through the harness, shaking it loosely to widen it, and then gripped the traces with the left... I sat hard, my whole weight crushing her into the sand'). R20's fight, while energetic, stays at a more generic highlight-reel level ('vaulted over the crouched pit lord, scorching the vanguard') without comparable embodied tracking.

proposals.name: Central premise delivered by implication, not declaration
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story makes the reader assemble its governing fact -- who or what the narrator is, what has actually happened, or what the situation means -- from evidence planted in the text, instead of stating it outright. CLEARLY SATISFYING: the key fact is never named, yet is unmistakably recoverable from consistent in-world vocabulary, from behaviour, or from a closing line that retro-fits everything before it; a careful reader finishes the piece knowing something the text never said. CLEARLY FAILING: narration announces the premise, a character explains the situation aloud to someone who would already know it, or an authorial aside glosses the joke for the reader. IMPORTANT GUARD: this is not a reward for vagueness. If a careful reader cannot reconstruct the withheld fact at all, score LOW, same as for over-explanation. Score only the presence of recoverable withheld information.
proposals.rationale: R06 never once uses the word for what the narrator is, but 'Great-Long-Lived', 'One-of-Nine' and 'the Field After' make it fully recoverable; R14 never states the narrator's ability, letting the question itself expose it; R02 withholds its whole reframe until five words on a screen. The opposite pole is where the scorecard is generous: R05 appends '(in the real world, there would probably be more emoji)', explaining its own joke, and R30 has one character lecture another about facility mechanics purely so the reader learns the stakes. A bank that scores clarity and completeness will credit R05/R30 and penalise R06/R14 exactly backwards.

proposals.name: Final beat reframes the piece rather than tagging out
proposals.instruction: Read only the last two or three sentences and ask what they do to everything before them. CLEARLY SATISFYING: the ending changes how the preceding text should be read, opens an irreversible consequence, or lands a meaning that was being built silently throughout; removing it would collapse the story. CLEARLY FAILING: the ending is a punchline that resolves nothing, a return to the exact status quo, a curtain line of the 'and so they went to the pub / ready for more misadventures' type, or an authorial sign-off standing in for an ending. Middle: a competent but predictable close that completes the scene without altering it.
proposals.rationale: R02 ends on 'We are here to help.' which retroactively turns a horror scene into an unresolved threat; R12 ends on a date and an unhinged jaw, converting a trauma monologue into body horror; R31 closes with Lady Deryn, which quietly indicts the whole custom. Against these, the scorecard-favoured rows close on tags that change nothing: R17 ends 'ready to commit more misadventures', R03 ends on 'Pub.', R09 ends on a stoner punchline that abandons the dragon statue. An ending-quality item scored as 'is there a satisfying conclusion' will pass all of these; the distinction that matters is whether the conclusion carries information.

proposals.name: Detail is selected for narrative work, not inventoried
proposals.instruction: Sample the concrete detail in the story and ask, of each item, whether it tells the reader something about character, pressure, or consequence that nothing else in the story tells. CLEARLY SATISFYING: physical specifics are load-bearing -- an object, a procedure, or a sensory fact reveals skill, fear, class, or history the narration never states -- and a reader could not delete them without losing meaning. CLEARLY FAILING: detail arrives as a catalogue or spec sheet (room contents, equipment functions, brand names, appearance lists) that is vivid but inert; the passage would read the same with the items swapped out. Do not reward quantity of description; reward the ratio of working detail to decorative detail.
proposals.rationale: R34's specifics -- the harness fed onto the right arm, the traces gripped left, sitting the hatchling down in hot sand -- simultaneously establish drilled competence and the fear the narrator is hiding; R20's smells and slivered moonlight all bear on the hunt. The card-favoured pole is dense with inert detail: R21 catalogues blue carpet, yellow walls, a racecar bed, a 32-inch flat screen, an Apple TV and a silver macbook without a single item doing work beyond decor, and R30 spends four paragraphs on what an atmospheric processor produces. Any 'vivid concrete sensory detail' item scores R21 and R30 near the top by volume alone.

proposals.name: Restraint at the emotional peak
proposals.instruction: Locate the story's highest-feeling moment (death, loss, betrayal, revelation) and judge how it is written. CLEARLY SATISFYING: the prose gets quieter, plainer or more concrete as feeling rises; the emotion is inferred by the reader from behaviour, physical fact or omission, and is not named. CLEARLY FAILING: the peak is carried by named emotions and body-fluid inventory ('her heart was breaking', 'wracked with pain', tears/mucus/shaking catalogued), by narration that states the character's inner realisation in explicit thematic language, or by intensifiers doing the work the scene should do.
proposals.rationale: R06 renders a death as 'Eventually I noticed the only heat was my own, and the paw had ceased moving' -- no feeling word anywhere; R28 lands its turn on eggs, bacon and a hope about tomorrow's refrigerator. On the other side, R13 stages grief with plastered hair, mucus, sobs and 'her heart was breaking', R33 writes 'rage ensnares Angie in its thorny coils', and R29 announces 'the inexpressible sorrow of one who has just learned that he is alone in the universe'. These are the fluent, legible emotional signals a criterion bank most reliably rewards, and they are precisely where the dense model backs off.

proposals.name: Form chosen for the material, not the default story shape
proposals.instruction: Ask whether the story's format -- prose scene, transcript, in-world document, verse, fragmented monologue, chat log -- is answerable to its content, and whether that form does work an ordinary scene could not. CLEARLY SATISFYING: the shape of the text enacts its subject (flat affect written in flat lines, repetition written as repetition, an argument staged as a document or a classroom exchange), and the choice earns something. CLEARLY FAILING: the piece defaults to a generic scene-plus-dialogue shape that fits the material no better than any other, or adopts an unusual format as decoration while the content ignores it. Do NOT penalise a story merely for lacking scene, dialogue, description or a conventional arc; judge the fit of the form that is there.
proposals.rationale: R16 writes emotional numbing in short, dropped, ellipsis-broken lines that make the reader feel the flattening; R28 counts '1, 2, 3. 1, 2, 3.' to enact its loop; R15 is a survival-manual extract whose dry institutional register is the joke; R32 is verse; R14 is a bare lecture transcript. All five are scored very low by the scorecard and very high by the dense model, which is the signature of a bank whose items presuppose prose scene, characters and dialogue. Compare R08 and R23, which apply a competent default scene shape to their material and are credited generously.

proposals.name: Register committed to and sustained end to end
proposals.instruction: Identify the register the story establishes in its first paragraph (liturgical, scholarly, mock-anthropological, deadpan procedural, hardboiled, etc.) and check whether it holds all the way through. CLEARLY SATISFYING: diction, syntax and comic distance stay inside one deliberate register for the whole piece, including the ending, and any shift is clearly purposeful and prepared. CLEARLY FAILING: an elevated or distinctive opening decays into ordinary narration; a sustained tone is punctured by an out-of-register joke or modern idiom that the story does not own; or the closing paragraphs read as though written for a different piece.
proposals.rationale: R31 holds a mock-ethnographic voice for its full length, down to the parenthetical on Alric Turnip; R06 sustains a liturgical register including its returning refrain; R15 never breaks the containment-protocol voice. Contrast R11, which opens on genuinely strong figurative writing ('stretched wide like the sighing of whales') and then drops into flat procedural narration for its second half, and R25, whose submarine-military pastiche is repeatedly punctured by kiddie-pool and mating-season gags. Sentence-level style items will credit R11's opening and R25's fluency without noticing that neither holds.

proposals.name: Attempts something that could plainly have failed
proposals.instruction: Ask what the writer risked. CLEARLY SATISFYING: the piece takes an identifiable formal, tonal or conceptual gamble -- a POV the reader must decode, verse, deliberately affectless prose, a repellent narrator, a joke sustained past the point of safety -- such that a plausible reader could reject it outright; the risk is executed on purpose, not by accident. CLEARLY FAILING: the piece executes a familiar template accurately and safely; nothing in it could have gone badly wrong. Note explicitly: surface correctness is not evidence for this criterion, and rough mechanics are not evidence against it -- judge the ambition of the attempt, then whether the attempt is carried through.
proposals.rationale: R32 answers a prose prompt in doggerel verse; R06 stakes the whole story on a POV riddle that fails completely if the reader does not decode it; R16 deliberately writes boring, drained sentences to convey a drained world; R12 lets its narrator become the thing it feared. All four sit near the bottom of the scorecard and near the top of the dense model. The low pole is where the scorecard is happiest: R01 executes a stock interrogation scene with a stock accent and a stock rescue, R08 executes an assigned trope tidily to a stated word count, R17 lifts a curse with no cost. Nothing in any of them could have failed.

proposals.name: Independence from borrowed characters and stock genre furniture
proposals.instruction: Ask how much of the story's effect is supplied by material the reader already owns. CLEARLY SATISFYING: the interest comes from invention specific to this piece -- its own custom, its own cosmology, its own comic logic -- and any borrowed element is bent into a new use. CLEARLY FAILING: recognition does the work: familiar characters imported for the pleasure of the crossover, standard-issue genre set dressing (the swinging bulb, the phonetically spelled enemy accent, the femme-fatale rescue), or clichés used straight rather than turned. A story may name its inherited premise from the writing prompt without penalty; judge what it adds beyond it.
proposals.rationale: R01 assembles a concrete cell, a dangling bulb it even calls cliche, an accent rendered as 'vat vas it', and a rescue by a woman who produces a pistol from her blouse; R29 runs on the reader's affection for two imported characters and largely restages a famous scene; R13 dresses its one gag in off-the-shelf breakup melodrama. All three are scored high by the scorecard. R31 by contrast invents an entire economic custom with its own history and R06 invents a whole devotional vocabulary; both are scored very low by the scorecard. Familiarity reads to an item-by-item judge as competence.

proposals.name: Prompt honoured as a constraint through to the ending
proposals.instruction: Compare the writing prompt with the story's last third, not its first. CLEARLY SATISFYING: the specific element the prompt names is still operative at the end -- it has been paid off, inverted, or deliberately refused in a way the story acknowledges -- so the prompt functions as a constraint on the whole piece. CLEARLY FAILING: the prompt supplies an opening image or licence and is then dropped, with the named element never used, or the story delivers a situation adjacent to the prompt while leaving its central specified event to happen offstage or not at all. Oblique or unexpected fulfilment counts as satisfying; abandonment does not.
proposals.rationale: R01 is prompted on a murderer offering a final phone call: a telephone sits on the table, is unplugged, and the call never happens. R09 is prompted on a statue that blinks; the statue blinks in the first line and is never seen again. Both are scored near the top by the scorecard. Compare R06, which is still discharging the prompt's honour-guard premise in its final line, R15, whose closing conference is the prompt's own logic played out, and R34, which ends on the consequence of the hatching it was asked for. Prompt fidelity checked only at the opening is a check the abandoners pass.

proposals.name: A character wants something they will not say
proposals.instruction: Ask whether any character carries an unstated want, fear or shame that shapes their behaviour on the page. CLEARLY SATISFYING: the reader can name a motive the character never names, and can point to specific lines where the motive leaks -- a rationalisation, an avoidance, a piece of overcompensation, a relief the character would deny. CLEARLY FAILING: characters want only what they say they want, or exist purely to deliver banter or plot; internal states, if present, are announced directly rather than betrayed. Score the presence of the gap between stated and actual, not the amount of introspection.
proposals.rationale: R34's narrator hopes the egg has died and presses their lips together to hide a smile, and only the last line admits the fear of flying; R10's Mason narrates gratitude to Kale while the resentment and dependence bleed through every clause; R40's narrator constructs an escalating justification for serial murder she never calls murder. All three are scorecard-low. The card-high pole is thin here: R17's dwarf and horse trade jokes with no interior life at all, and R09's two characters exist to set up a punchline. A 'characterisation' item satisfied by distinct speech patterns will not separate these.

proposals.name: Beats escalate; the situation becomes irreversible
proposals.instruction: Track the story's beats in order and ask whether each one changes the situation. CLEARLY SATISFYING: pressure compounds -- new information, new cost, or a closed-off option at each turn -- so that by the end something cannot be undone. CLEARLY FAILING: the same beat repeats with variation but no increase (a gag performed three or four times at the same intensity), or events occur and leave the world exactly as it was found. A story may be static by design if the stasis is the subject, but then the stasis must be doing work the reader can name.
proposals.rationale: R12 escalates from a defensive war story to a confession to an appetite; R34 raises the cost of the hatching with each death and ends the narrator locked into a life they dread; R02 tightens from a flickering lamp to a body to a message. Against these, R13 stages the same wall-licking joke four times at identical intensity while the emotional description grows louder rather than the situation changing, and R09 and R26 both end where they began. Repetition with escalating adjectives reads as rising action to a per-item judge; it is not.

proposals.name: Story uses real working knowledge of its domain
proposals.instruction: Ask whether the writer knows something specific and true about the world they are writing in, and whether the story uses that knowledge rather than gesturing at it. CLEARLY SATISFYING: a real mechanism, procedure or argument is deployed accurately and drives a scene -- an actual technical objection, a handling procedure, a strategic logic that follows through. CLEARLY FAILING: domain material is present but hand-waved, decorative or self-contradictory, or arrives as an explanatory lecture that never constrains anyone's choices. Fantastical settings qualify: the test is internal rigour and consequence, not real-world accuracy.
proposals.rationale: R14's student raises a genuine objective-collapse objection -- the geiger counter as an in-box observer -- and that argument is the entire story; R34 knows how a frightened animal is bridled and sat down; R15 reasons correctly from light-lag and cheap Oort-cloud bolides to a first-exposure-first-extinction equilibrium and then to the reversal. All three are scored near the bottom by the scorecard. Compare R22, whose astronomy is asserted and hand-waved, and R30, whose long specification of the processor never constrains anyone until it is shouted as exposition.

proposals.name: Moral discomfort left standing, not resolved for the reader
proposals.instruction: Ask whether the story leaves the reader holding something unpleasant. CLEARLY SATISFYING: the piece commits to a perspective the reader cannot comfortably endorse -- a narrator whose reasoning is coherent and wrong, cruelty rendered without editorial distancing, an ending that refuses to adjudicate -- and does not supply a character or line that tells the reader how to feel. CLEARLY FAILING: the moral is stated, the transgressor is punished or reformed on cue, or a figure of authority appears to articulate the rules and the lesson. Judge refusal to resolve, not shock content: gore or profanity alone satisfies nothing.
proposals.rationale: R12 ends with the narrator's new hunger presented as pleasure, with no correction offered; R40 keeps its unrepentant murderer sympathetic to the last line; R07 lets an author torture his own creation for entertainment and signs off 'Well...that was fun :)'. All three are scorecard-low. The scorecard-high pole tidies up: R08's angel states 'We have rules' and the story delivers exact karmic symmetry, and R03 resolves its transgression into companionable warmth. Items rewarding thematic clarity and a satisfying resolution will systematically prefer the tidied version.

proposals.name: Freestanding fiction: a situation exists, no external context needed
proposals.instruction: Two joined tests, both required for a high score. (1) IS IT FICTION AT ALL: is there a person or agent in a situation, with something happening to them or being decided by them? (2) IS IT FREESTANDING: can a reader who has only the writing prompt and this text get everything they need, without a prior instalment, a contest round, community membership, or knowledge of a subreddit's procedures? CLEARLY SATISFYING: a self-sufficient dramatic situation with no external dependency. CLEARLY FAILING: administrative, announcement or moderation prose with no situation at all; or a story whose opening line directs the reader elsewhere to understand it, or whose framing assumes participation in a community process. Housekeeping sign-offs after a complete story do not count against this; dependency inside the story does.
proposals.rationale: R38 is an automated moderation removal notice containing no story whatever, and it is scored in the top fifth by the scorecard -- decisive evidence that the bank's items can be satisfied by clear, purposeful, correctly toned prose that is not fiction. R18 is a moderator explainer about a monthly feature, likewise not a story. R01 opens by declaring itself 'a continuation of a series of earlier prompt responses' and links out for the context it withholds; R11 is a contest heat that closes by congratulating other participants. All of the dependent rows sit high on the scorecard and low on the dense model.

proposals.name: Voice individuates a person, not dialect costume
proposals.instruction: Ask what the story's distinctive speech is carrying. CLEARLY SATISFYING: the idiom is the character -- word choice, evasions, rhythm and what the speaker declines to say reveal their history, self-image or blind spots, and could not be transferred to another character without loss. CLEARLY FAILING: the distinctiveness is an accent or a register applied as costume -- phonetic respelling, dialect tics, texting abbreviations, catchphrases -- carrying group identity but no individual information, such that any member of the group would speak the same lines. Assess how much of the voice survives if you strip the spelling gimmicks; if nothing remains, score low.
proposals.rationale: R40's narrator gives herself away through the very idiom she reassures herself with ('you know how girls are', 'I was good'); R16's flattened, trailing sentences are the speaker's condition; R06's honorifics and refrain constitute a whole worldview. Against these, R26 is written almost entirely in surfer respellings ('brah', 'totes', 'gnarly') that identify a type and nothing more, R01 renders its interrogator as 'I vill say vat I please', and R05 is chat-shorthand with no person behind either handle. A distinctive-voice item counts the tics and credits the costume.

proposals.name: Prompt-to-plot transformation
proposals.instruction: Score how deeply the prompt’s unusual premise drives the conflict, character choices, and resolution. Score high when removing the premise would collapse the story; score low when it is only mentioned or used for a detached gag.
proposals.rationale: R02 makes science and magic jointly determine the confrontation, while R25 turns broadcasting into the central strategic mechanism. By contrast, R40 largely uses its prompt line as a late accusation rather than as the story’s governing engine.

proposals.name: Earned recontextualization
proposals.instruction: Score whether a later revelation meaningfully changes the interpretation of earlier details and is prepared by prior evidence. Score high when the reversal feels inevitable in retrospect; score low when it is merely announced or appended at the end.
proposals.rationale: R05’s infection reveal transforms the narrator’s earlier testimony, and R30’s shifting domestic reality gradually exposes the coma. R09’s final testing message and R14’s final joke provide comparatively little preparation or reinterpretation.

proposals.name: Character-specific voice
proposals.instruction: Score whether diction, rhythm, figurative language, and attitude create a distinctive voice appropriate to the character or narrator. Score high when the voice remains controlled and individualized; score low when it is generic or depends on one repeated verbal gimmick.
proposals.rationale: R15 sustains an arch satirical voice, and R36 makes customer-service jargon feel characterful within its fantasy setting. R08 and R21 instead rely heavily on repetitive stoner or surfer speech without comparable development.

proposals.name: Behavioral interior conflict
proposals.instruction: Score how convincingly the story shows contradictory feelings through behavior, perception, or choice rather than merely naming emotions. Score high when inner conflict complicates the character’s actions; score low when emotion is stated without psychological movement.
proposals.rationale: R03 conveys devotion, grief, and denial through the guard’s rituals, while R38 dramatizes resentment through Mason’s changing reactions to violence. R19 repeatedly labels distress without developing the characters’ underlying conflict.

proposals.name: Embedded worldbuilding
proposals.instruction: Score whether setting rules and social structures emerge naturally through action, sensory detail, and consequences. Score high when exposition is inseparable from the scene; score low when the story pauses for lists of facts, terminology, or background.
proposals.rationale: R18 reveals dragon-training customs through dangerous physical behavior, and R36 integrates magical rules into an ordinary support call. R37 and R40 provide extensive explanatory background that is only loosely embodied in immediate action.

proposals.name: Causal consequence chain
proposals.instruction: Score whether major events produce clear changes in circumstances, options, or behavior, leading coherently to the ending. Score high when each important beat creates the next; score low when scenes or ideas could be rearranged without affecting the outcome.
proposals.rationale: R02’s scientific spells alter the tactical situation step by step, and R34’s server-room discovery follows from a concrete sequence of failures. R28 and R40 contain events whose consequences are comparatively loose or delayed.

proposals.name: Narrative economy
proposals.instruction: Score whether the story spends words on details that advance character, tension, setting, or theme. Score high when repetition and setup are purposeful; score low when boilerplate, promotion, recap, or redundant explanation displaces the story.
proposals.rationale: R16 creates a complete premise-and-ending arc in very few lines, while R35 moves efficiently from interrogation to reversal. R10 is almost entirely boilerplate, and R40 devotes substantial space to exposition before the immediate conflict.

proposals.name: Fresh trope transformation
proposals.instruction: Score whether familiar genre elements are transformed into a specific social, emotional, or conceptual situation. Score high when the novelty comes from the implications of the premise; score low when the story merely assembles recognizable tropes or names.
proposals.rationale: R03 reframes humans as revered long-lived beings through an animal’s worldview, and R15 turns romantic fantasy convention into an economic institution. R01 and R20 mainly combine familiar genre properties without equally distinctive consequences.

proposals.name: Resonant closing image
proposals.instruction: Score whether the final line or image crystallizes the story’s central tension and adds meaning beyond simple stopping or surprise. Score high when the ending lingers and echoes earlier material; score low when it is generic, abrupt, or merely a disconnected punchline.
proposals.rationale: R03’s repeated service refrain gains new meaning after the death, and R31’s disappearance into the dream completes the protector’s role. R12 and R28 end on pleasant jokes that do not substantially deepen what came before.

proposals.name: Sentence-level control
proposals.instruction: Score grammatical correctness, syntactic clarity, word precision, and readable rhythm. Score high when the prose feels deliberately shaped; score low when errors, malformed sentences, or awkward phrasing repeatedly interrupt comprehension.
proposals.rationale: R15, R31, and R35 maintain polished, controlled sentences while handling complex scenes. R13, R30, and R37 contain frequent grammatical or usage problems that weaken otherwise understandable premises.

proposals.name: Tonal calibration
proposals.instruction: Score how well humor, horror, sentiment, suspense, and seriousness are balanced for the story’s intended effect. Score high when tonal shifts are motivated and controlled; score low when emotional treatment clashes with the situation or becomes one-note.
proposals.rationale: R05 combines bodily horror with disturbing comic detachment, and R35 balances banter against physical danger. R19 and R21 repeatedly pair heightened emotional framing with deliberately silly behavior in ways that flatten the intended effect.

proposals.name: Agency under constraint
proposals.instruction: Score whether the protagonist makes consequential choices despite meaningful limitations, and whether those choices alter the story. Score high when decisions reveal character and carry costs; score low when the protagonist mainly observes events or acts without changing the trajectory.
proposals.rationale: R02 makes Alfred’s scientific knowledge decisive, and R18’s fear and family duty force the rider into a dangerous choice. R13’s narrator is largely carried by confusion, while R17’s protagonist disappears before his own investigation can resolve.

proposals.name: Reciprocal relationships
proposals.instruction: Score whether important relationships contain distinct wants, mutual influence, and behavior that reveals the bond. Score high when connection is dramatized through interaction; score low when relationships are asserted, one-sided, or reduced to interchangeable banter.
proposals.rationale: R03 builds the bond between guardian and Great-Long-Lived through reciprocal care, and R35 makes the rescue depend on an established partnership. R19 and R39 present relationships largely through labels or superficial exchanges.

proposals.name: Moral self-implication
proposals.instruction: Score whether the protagonist or narrator recognizes complicity, rationalization, or morally conflicting motives. Score high when the story resists a simple moral division; score low when harmful behavior is excused by a single justification or flattened into stock villainy.
proposals.rationale: R05 gradually reveals the narrator’s complicity in spreading danger, and R38 exposes resentment beneath Mason’s apparently practical role. R06 and R32 largely justify destructive behavior through revenge while leaving limited moral uncertainty.

proposals.name: Form serving content
proposals.instruction: Score whether the chosen structure or presentation embodies the premise, controls information, or creates meaning. Score high when form and subject reinforce each other; score low when a transcript, document, chat, or poem is merely a container for ordinary exposition.
proposals.rationale: R04’s fragmented counting enacts the time loop, and R25’s survival-document format makes its strategic perspective meaningful. R10’s automated-message format contains no developing narrative, while R39’s chat format mainly reproduces the prompt superficially.

proposals.name: Premise-to-Plot Transformation
proposals.instruction: Score high when the prompt's unusual element generates specific conflict, choices, and meaning; score low when it is merely mentioned or used as decorative genre dressing.
proposals.rationale: R14 and R24 make the speculative premise reshape the entire situation and worldview, whereas R01 and R25 barely develop their prompts.

proposals.name: Causal Escalation
proposals.instruction: Score high when each event changes the available options or raises the stakes toward the ending; score low when episodes are interchangeable, disconnected, or only narrated as background.
proposals.rationale: R09, R28, and R39 build consequences step by step, while R10 and R33 largely present isolated exchanges without meaningful escalation.

proposals.name: Subtextual Character Conflict
proposals.instruction: Score high when desires, resentments, loyalties, or fears emerge through behavior and implication as well as dialogue; score low when characters simply announce flat motives or stereotypes.
proposals.rationale: R04 and R34 communicate conflicted loyalties through thought and action, unlike the largely declared emotional positions in R15 and R16.

proposals.name: Earned Recontextualizing Reveal
proposals.instruction: Score high when a reversal or revelation changes the meaning of earlier details and has been quietly prepared; score low when it arrives arbitrarily or adds shock without reinterpretation.
proposals.rationale: R08, R23, and R37 seed later revelations in earlier observations, whereas R18 and R35 end with developments that feel appended rather than prepared.

proposals.name: Form That Enacts the Premise
proposals.instruction: Score high when structure, formatting, diction, or narration makes the prompt's underlying concept happen on the page; score low when the same prose form could serve any unrelated premise.
proposals.rationale: R13's poem, R20's recursive dialogue, and R32's counting structure embody their premises, while R05 and R40 use conventional exposition for highly conceptual prompts.

proposals.name: Selective Sensory Specificity
proposals.instruction: Score high when concrete sensory details are distinctive, selective, and reveal character, danger, or setting; score low when details are generic, ornamental, or piled on without function.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R24 use smell, texture, heat, and touch to deepen their situations, while R06 and R38 often accumulate descriptive details without comparable narrative leverage.

proposals.name: Second-Order Worldbuilding
proposals.instruction: Score high when the premise plausibly changes institutions, customs, incentives, or everyday behavior beyond the immediate scene; score low when the setting is only a backdrop or an information dump.
proposals.rationale: R14, R30, and R40 extrapolate their premises into social systems and historical behavior, whereas R05 mostly explains its world without dramatizing its consequences.

proposals.name: Moral Ambivalence
proposals.instruction: Score high when competing values make the protagonist's actions understandable yet troubling, with no easy moral resolution; score low when heroes, villains, and motives remain morally simple.
proposals.rationale: R09, R18, and R34 create discomfort around violence, responsibility, and protection, unlike the straightforward revenge logic of R15 and the binary conflict in R38.

proposals.name: Distinctive, Controlled Voice
proposals.instruction: Score high when narration has a memorable perspective whose tone remains intentional and can modulate for contrast; score low when voice is generic or a repeated gimmick overwhelms characterization.
proposals.rationale: R13, R24, and R30 sustain highly recognizable voices, while R02 and R35 repeat surface quirks until they replace rather than express personality.

proposals.name: Dramatized Exposition
proposals.instruction: Score high when necessary context is revealed through consequential action, conflict, or purposeful dialogue; score low when long explanatory passages delay the scene and could be removed without changing events.
proposals.rationale: R03, R21, and R39 disclose rules and history during immediate danger, whereas R05 and R40 front-load extensive explanation before meaningful dramatic movement.

proposals.name: Costly Character Agency
proposals.instruction: Score high when a character makes a consequential choice that reflects a specific desire or fear and creates a real cost; score low when the protagonist mainly observes, reacts, or succeeds without sacrifice.
proposals.rationale: R28, R34, and R39 turn decisive personal choices into danger or obligation, while R08 and R22 leave their narrators largely passive within unfolding circumstances.

proposals.name: Narrative Economy
proposals.instruction: Score high when nearly every paragraph or exchange advances plot, character, atmosphere, or meaning; score low when repetition, padding, meta-commentary, or catalogued setup dilutes the central movement.
proposals.rationale: R13 and R32 achieve substantial effect through compression, whereas R01, R05, and R27 devote much of their space to repetition, setup, or non-story material.

proposals.name: Fresh Image Precision
proposals.instruction: Score high when figurative language is surprising, apt, and easy to visualize; score low when imagery relies on stock comparisons, mixes incompatible metaphors, or obscures the action.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R13 make unusual images carry atmosphere and concept, while R31 and R38 show how dense figurative or sensational language can become confusing rather than clarifying.

proposals.name: Self-Contained Narrative Payoff
proposals.instruction: Score high when the presented text establishes enough context, completes a meaningful arc, and lands on an earned endpoint; score low when it depends on prior installments, promotional framing, moderation text, or an unresolved setup.
proposals.rationale: R03, R23, and R28 provide intelligible arcs within the excerpt, whereas R07, R25, R26, and R27 rely on meta-context, continuation, or failure to produce a complete story.

proposals.name: Productive Ambiguity
proposals.instruction: Score high when uncertainty invites inference while recurring clues keep the possibilities coherent; score low when confusion comes from missing context, unstable references, or arbitrary surreal events.
proposals.rationale: R23, R31, and R32 make disorientation part of a patterned experience, while R22, R35, and R38 more often leave uncertainty without a reliable interpretive structure.
